items.summary: दिल्ली में प्रदूषण को नियंत्रित करने के लिए सरकार हर साल सर्दियों में ‘विंटर एक्शन प्लान’ लागू करती है. इसके तहत निर्माण कार्यों समेत कई गतिविधियों पर रोक लगाई जाती है. इस रोक का असर सबसे ज्यादा उन निर्माण मजदूरों पर पड़ता है, जिनकी रोजी-रोटी हर रोज की कमाई पर निर्भर है. निर्माण कार्य बंद होने के बाद उनके पास रोजगार का कोई दूसरा साधन नहीं बचता. कई मजदूरों को दो महीने तक काम नहीं मिलता. राजमिस्त्री और दिहाड़ी मजदूरों के लिए इस दौरान कहीं और काम ढूंढना भी मुश्किल हो जाता है. इसी समस्या को देखते हुए सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने 24 नवंबर 2021 के अपने आदेश में निर्माण कार्यों पर रोक के दौरान प्रभावित मजदूरों को आर्थिक सहायता देने का निर्देश दिया था. इसके बाद दिल्ली के मंत्री कपिल मिश्रा ने दिसंबर 2025 में घोषणा की थी कि काम बंद होने से प्रभावित मजदूरों को 10,000 रुपये का मुआवजा दिया जाएगा. न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री ने कुुछ ऐसे निर्माण मजदूरों से बात की, जिन्होंने करीब दो साल पहले दिल्ली बिल्डिंग एंड अदर कंस्ट्रक्शन वर्कर्स वेलफेयर बोर्ड में अपना रजिस्ट्रेशन कराया था. लेकिन इन मजदूरों का दावा है कि उन्हें अब तक मुआवजा नहीं मिला है. देखिए ये रिपोर्ट. एक स्वतंत्र मीडिया जिन सवालों के जवाब मिलने चाहिए उन सवालों को पूछ कर जनतंत्र को थामे रखता है, जिन कहानियों को कहना जरूरी है उन्हें कह कर उसे बचाए रखता है. स्वतंत्र पत्रकारिता का समर्थन करें. आज ही सब्सक्राइब करें. 8 घंटे काम, हफ्ते में एक दिन छुट्टी और बेहतर वेतन के लिए दो महीने से लड़ रहे सूरत के कपड़ा मजदूर ग्रेटर नोएडा: सर्विस लिफ्ट गिरने से नाबालिग सहित आठ की मौत और पलायन को मजबूर मजदूर

items.title: Friends of the liver: Punjab’s quiet epidemic of male heartbreak
items.summary: In Punjab, a pair of lifelong best friends are called jigri yaar : friends joined not merely at the heart but at the liver. The phrase suggests an intimacy so deep it is almost anatomical, as if friendship has passed beyond feeling and entered the body. Punjabi songs and Hindi films have long celebrated this kind of male devotion: two men eating from the same plate, sleeping under the same quilt, risking death for each other, calling each other brother because no other word is available. What these stories rarely make room for is what happens when one of those men leaves. For those of us who came of age in the 1990s, before terms like gay, lesbian, and bisexual entered our vocabulary, these portrayals of fraternal love provided rare openings. They allowed us to expand our suppressed desires into the realm of fantasy. Queer philosopher Judith Butler has argued that fantasy is not the opposite of reality but rather shaped by it, filling in what reality so frequently denies. For queer men like me, such fantasies created possibilities beyond what was immediately available. Watching men on-screen display affection toward one another was not only an escape from the overwhelming weight of patriarchal expectations. It was also a glimpse of something else that might be possible, even if only fleeting: that love between two men could be imagined. During my fieldwork in Indian Punjab, I began to hear another story underneath these familiar celebrations of male friendship. The story was not simply about desire, or secrecy, or the impossibility of naming certain forms of love. It was also about migration. Again and again, men spoke of friends who had left: for Canada, for the United States, for Australia, for the Gulf. These departures were described by families as success, as sacrifice, as a son’s chance to rescue the household from debt. But, for the friends left behind, they often felt like abandonment. items.title: No work, little compensation: Delhi’s construction workers pay the price for its toxic air
items.summary: Delhi’s air pollution worsens every winter, prompting the government to impose restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP). These include halting construction work and restricting the entry of certain vehicles. But when construction sites shut down, it is migrant workers who bear the brunt. With no work or alternative source of income, many go weeks, sometimes months, without a wage. Some are forced to return to their villages with their children because they can no longer afford to stay in Delhi. In a November 24, 2021 order, the Supreme Court directed the government to provide financial assistance to workers affected by construction bans. In December 2025, Delhi minister Kapil Mishra announced compensation of Rs 10,000 for workers who lost work due to GRAP restrictions. Newslaundry spoke to construction workers who say they had registered with the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board nearly two years ago and renewed their registrations on time, but have still not received the promised compensation. The board says around one lakh workers have been paid, at a cost of nearly Rs 100 crore. Its website lists around 2.15 lakh registered workers. The Construction Workers Panchayat Sangam, a union representing construction workers, has filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court claiming that around 1,700 workers are still awaiting compensation. The court’s 2024 order also referred to financial assistance for 93,272 construction workers in Delhi. According to a CEEW report , construction activities account for around 30 percent of Delhi’s dust pollution. But while the government acts against pollution, it is the workers who lose their livelihoods. This report is part of a collaborative campaign to tackle air pollution. items.title: Ola's extra pay for faster rides feature doesn't work: CCPA asks it to scrap practice, slaps ₹10 lakh penalty
items.summary: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 lakh on ANI Technologies Private Limited, which operates Ola, for misleading consumers into paying additional amounts to improve their chances of securing a ride. In an order dated November 10, the CCPA held that Ola's practice of prompting customers to pay extra before a driver accepted their booking amounted to a misleading advertisement, unfair trade practice and unfair contract under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Hence, it ordered the platform to stop the feature/ practice while also imposing a penalty on it. The order was passed by Chief Commissioner Nidhi Khare and Commissioner Anupam Mishra . The proceedings arose from a complaint received in May 2025 concerning Ola's advance tipping feature. While customers waited for a driver to accept their booking, the app displayed messages suggesting that paying an additional amount could improve their chances of securing a ride. One such prompt stated: "Adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster." Customers were initially offered pre-set amounts ranging from ₹10 to ₹40, which subsequently increased. The Authority found that the application permitted add-on amounts of up to ₹499. Ola defended the feature, arguing that the additional payment was voluntary and transferred directly to drivers without any deduction by the platform. items.title: Is the Collegium system failing women?
items.summary: Proportional representation is fundamental to a democratic society. The legitimacy of public institutions depends not merely on their independence, but also on whether people from different sections of society have a meaningful opportunity to participate in them. This becomes particularly important in the judiciary, where representation influences not only institutional diversity, but also public confidence in the administration of justice. The persistent underrepresentation of women in India's higher judiciary, therefore, demands serious examination. Recently on October 6, 2026, Justice Sunita Agarwal took oath as a judge of the Supreme Court of India, only the 13th woman to be appointed to the Court in its history. Her appointment increased the number of women judges from two to three, against a working strength of 37 judges. Women, therefore, constitute just 8.1 per cent of the Supreme Court's strength. More than seven decades after its establishment, the country's highest judicial institution continues to have a strikingly poor record of women's representation. The figures present a striking disparity across various High Courts. According to the Ministry of Law and Justice , 7,852 women officers occupy positions against a sanctioned strength of 25,886 across district and subordinate courts, accounting for approximately 38 per cent as of February 2025. State-level figures reveal even higher concentrations: Goa records around 70 per cent, while Meghalaya and Nagaland hover near 63 per cent. However, the representation declines considerably at the higher levels. A press release issued by the Ministry on February 2, 2026 , reported that women constituted only 116 of the 814 working judges across the High Courts. The Punjab and Haryana High Court had 18 women judges out of 61, Bombay had 12 out of 80, while Delhi and Madras had 10 each. Several High Courts - including those of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh and Patna - had only two women judges each. The High Courts of Meghalaya, Odisha, Sikkim, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Himachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh had only one woman judge each, while Manipur, Tripura and Uttarakhand had none. These numbers form an inverted pyramid broader at the lower judiciary level and tapering at the higher judiciary level. items.title: Business development in law firms: How it builds client flow in India and internationally
items.summary: Ask most lawyers what wins a client and you will hear about the excellence of the work. That is only half the story. Before a client can judge the work, someone must introduce the firm, understand the client's problem and keep the relationship alive long after the file is closed. Increasingly, that someone is the business development (BD) team. BD is no longer a side activity for partners with spare time. It is a discipline of its own. This article looks at how BD works within India's advertising restrictions, how firms build visibility, and what it takes to win and keep clients at home and overseas. Why business development matters more than ever Work once reached Indian law firms through reputation and referrals. A founder's name, a few well-known deals and word of mouth did most of the job. That still works, but clients have changed. General counsel and overseas companies now compare firms on how quickly they respond, how clearly they price and how well they understand the business, not just the statute. BD sits in the middle of this. A good team studies the market, prepares pitches, manages directory submissions, and tells the firm which opportunities fit. Working within Rule 36: Visibility without advertising This is not a normal marketing job. Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules bars advocates from soliciting work or advertising, directly or indirectly. Since a 2008 amendment, firms may publish limited, factual details on a website. In March 2025, the Bar Council again warned against promotional videos, influencer endorsements and celebrity-led advertising. Until that changes, every firm works within the rule. The result is what practitioners call invisible marketing: useful content, conference speaking slots, commentary on legal developments and careful rankings submissions. A well-timed note on a court ruling that affects foreign investors can do more than a drawer full of brochures. The skill lies in knowing where informing the public ends and soliciting begins. items.title: Advocates and court staff perform essential duties: Delhi HC says while exempting them from non-BS VI vehicle ban
items.summary: The government has failed to explain how non-BS VI vehicles have suddenly become a major contributor to pollution, the Delhi High Court observed while exempting lawyers and court staff working in Delhi courts from the ban. Justice Amit Mahajan noted that these vehicles were allowed in the capital till last month. "The respondents have also not been able to point out, at this stage, how the same vehicles which were though not contributing to the pollution till the month of October, are suddenly being considered as a major contributor to the pollution," the Court observed. It added that advocates and court staff perform essential duties. "Once the Courts are functional, the Advocates and the Court staff’s attendance is, undoubtedly, of utmost importance for the smooth functioning of the Court and they cannot be directed to not ply their vehicles. It is not the case of the respondents that they have been providing adequate transport to the Advocates and the Court staff for coming to the Courts," Justice Mahajan said. Therefore, the Court said that the cars of advocates and court staff holding a valid parking sticker of any of the bar associations in Delhi will be permitted to travel to and from Delhi during court working days from November 1 to January 31, 2027. Justice Mahajan passed the order on a plea filed by the Delhi High Court Bar Association (DHCBA). Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court Senior Advocate N Hariharan had appeared for the DHCBA and argued that lawyers and judicial staff perform essential functions. He said that the government’s notification already has provisions to exempt certain categories of vehicles. He added that such exemptions were granted to lawyers even during the Covid-19 pandemic. “They [the government] have the power to exempt. As far as lawyers and court staff are concerned, we are performing judicial function and assisting My Lords. If we can’t come here, it will affect the entire justice delivery function,” Hariharan stated. Hariharan is also the president of DHCBA. items.title: TVK MLA accused of sending obscene messages to Kallakurichi Collector: Can POSH Act be used?
items.summary: C Arul Vignesh, the TVK MLA from Kallakurichi has been accused of sending obscene WhatsApp messages to Kallakurichi District Collector JE Padmaja. But the legislator has denied the allegations and blamed the opposition for playing “dirty politics”. However, a report by The New Indian Express quoted Villupuram range DIG A Arularasu who revealed that the MLA had reportedly misbehaved with the Collector nearly two months ago. The present allegations are yet to be verified, the DIG told the newspaper. Though the Collector has not filed a police complaint against the TVK MLA, reports suggest that Collector JE Padmaja had complained to higher officials about the MLA’s behaviour. The allegations also raise questions about whether the Prevention of Sexual Harassment (POSH) Act, 2013, can be invoked in this case. When TNM asked a senior IAS officer if a PoSH (Prevention of Sexual Harassment) Committee, officially known as the Internal Committee (IC), under the POSH Act of 2013, could intervene, he said that would require an official complaint from the Collector or someone on behalf of her. However, there is an inherent complication, the officer pointed out. Though there are POSH committees in every Collectorate, it is headed by the Collector. In this case therefore, the Collector will have to approach the Legislature or the government to lodge a POSH complaint. She also has the option of filing a police complaint. Meanwhile addressing the media on Tuesday, November 10, Arul Vignesh denied sending any inappropriate WhatsApp message to the Kallakurichi Collector. “Everyone came to know about the rumours spread through social media. I have always maintained high respect for government officers. False messages are being spread against me on social media,” he claimed. A day earlier, DMK MP Kanimozhi alleged that the TVK MLA stalked the Collector and tried trespassing into her residence. He also sent her obscene messages and trespassed into the Collector’s house, she alleged. “Reports are circulating on social media that TVK MLA Arul Vignesh sent obscene text messages to the District Collector of Kallakurichi, went to the collector’s home while drunk and harassed them, and that a dedicated security officer was subsequently assigned to the Collector.” “Under this incompetent TVK administration, law and order has broken down across Tamil Nadu, with murders, robberies and other crimes occurring one after another.
